---
title: "Files, keys and joins"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

An SRTR analysis usually combines several standard analysis files (SAFs):
transplants with their follow-up forms, recipients with their donors,
candidates with the transplants they went on to receive. Each file has its
own unit, and each join can multiply or drop rows without any error. This
article shows which identifier links which files, and how to check a join
before you trust it.

The examples use a few made-up rows, so they run on this site. The checks
work the same on your own files.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
```

# What are you counting?

Every count in an SRTR analysis counts something. Say which.

| Unit | Identifier | Found in | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Waitlist registration | `PX_ID` | `CAND_*`, `STATHIST_*`, `TX_*`, `TXF_*` | One person can be listed more than once, at several centers or for several organs |
| Person | `PERS_ID` | `CAND_*`, `TX_*`, `TXF_*` | A person transplanted twice has two transplant registrations |
| Transplant registration | `TRR_ID` | `TX_*`, `TXF_*`, `IMMUNO` | One per recipient per transplant registration |
| Transplant event | `TX_ID` | `TX_*`, `TXF_*` | Labelled "set same for multi\_org": one transplant event can have registrations in several organ files |
| Follow-up form | `TRR_FOL_ID` | `TXF_*`, `FOL_IMMUNO`, `MALIG`, `TREATMENT` | Several per transplant registration |
| Donor | `DONOR_ID` | `DONOR_DECEASED`, `DONOR_LIVE`, `TX_*`, `CAND_*` | A deceased donor can give organs to several recipients |
| Center | `CTR_ID` | `INSTITUTION` | Transplant files hold center identifiers such as `REC_CTR_ID` |

The `*` stands for an organ code, such as `TX_KI` for kidney or `CAND_LIIN`
for liver and intestine.

Two more links are easy to miss. `CAND_*` files hold `PERS_NEXTTX_TRR_ID`,
the transplant registration that followed a listing. And `PERS_ID` also
appears in the donor files, with its own label: read it in the data
dictionary before joining a donor file on `PERS_ID`.

These roles come from the variable labels in the SRTR data dictionary
(`sRtr::dictionary`). The labels are not always consistent: in the
dictionary, `TRR_ID` is called a "unique key" in follow-up files too, where
it repeats on every form. So check each key on your own files before you
rely on it, as below.

# Check a key before you join on it

A key should be present and unique in the file it identifies. Here is a
made-up transplant file and its follow-up forms:

```{r data}
tx <- tibble(
  TRR_ID = c(101, 102, 103, 104, 106, 107, 108),
  PERS_ID = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 3),
  DONOR_ID = c(51, 52, 51, 53, NA, 54, 55),
  REC_TX_DT = as.Date(c(
    "2015-03-01", "2019-06-01", "2015-03-02", "2018-01-01", "2020-05-01",
    "2018-01-01", "2018-01-01"
  ))
)
txf <- tibble(
  TRR_FOL_ID = 1:7,
  TRR_ID = c(101, 101, 102, 103, 103, 103, 105),
  TFL_PX_STAT_DT = as.Date(c(
    "2016-03-01", "2017-03-01", "2020-06-01",
    "2016-03-02", "2017-03-02", "2018-03-02", "2021-01-01"
  ))
)
```

Person 1 has two transplants (registrations 101 and 102). Donor 51 gave
organs to two recipients. Registration 106 has no donor identifier.
Person 3 has three registrations dated the same day (104, 107 and 108), a
made-up tie. One follow-up form (registration 105) has no transplant in
this file.

Check that the key is complete and unique:

```{r unique}
c(
  missing = sum(is.na(tx$TRR_ID)),
  repeated = sum(duplicated(tx$TRR_ID))
)
```

Both should be 0. Then check how the two files match:

```{r match}
c(
  forms_missing_key = sum(is.na(txf$TRR_ID)),
  forms_without_transplant = sum(!is.na(txf$TRR_ID) & !txf$TRR_ID %in% tx$TRR_ID),
  transplants_without_forms = sum(!tx$TRR_ID %in% txf$TRR_ID)
)
```

Count missing keys apart from known keys with no match: they have
different explanations. None of these has to be 0, but each needs an
explanation. A transplant without
forms may be too recent for its first follow-up, or lost to follow-up. A
form without a transplant usually means the transplant file was filtered
first, or comes from another organ.

On real files, print these counts with the masking helpers in
[Share counts only](checking-your-safs.html#share-counts-only), and keep
the totals for yourself.

# Count rows before and after every join

A join that should keep one row per transplant must not change the number
of transplants:

```{r join-donor}
donors <- tibble(
  DONOR_ID = c(51, 52, 53, 54, 55, NA),
  DON_AGE = c(40, 22, 61, 30, 45, 35)
)

tx_donor <- left_join(tx, donors, by = "DONOR_ID",
                      relationship = "many-to-one", na_matches = "never")
c(before = nrow(tx), after = nrow(tx_donor))
# A transplant with no donor identifier gets no donor values.
stopifnot(all(is.na(tx_donor$DON_AGE[is.na(tx_donor$DONOR_ID)])))
```

Three arguments do the work:

- `relationship = "many-to-one"` makes dplyr stop with an error if a donor
  appears twice in `donors`, instead of silently duplicating transplants.
- `na_matches = "never"` stops a missing key from matching a missing key.
  dplyr's default lets them match, so registration 106 would take the age
  of the donor record with no identifier. Here its donor age stays missing.
- `by` names the key. Never let a join pick its own columns: the
  transplant and donor files share many columns besides `DONOR_ID`.

Use the first two whenever each row should find at most one match.

Joining follow-up forms is different: the result has one row per form, not
per transplant.

```{r join-forms}
forms <- inner_join(tx, txf, by = "TRR_ID",
                    relationship = "one-to-many", na_matches = "never")
c(transplants = n_distinct(forms$TRR_ID), rows = nrow(forms))
```

Counting rows of `forms` counts forms. To count transplants with an event,
count distinct `TRR_ID`, or summarize to one row per transplant first.
`add_txf_outcomes()` does this for malignancy and rejection; see
[Follow-up forms](follow-up-forms.html).

# Columns in both files

Transplant files repeat many donor columns. In the dictionary, `TX_KI`
and `DONOR_DECEASED` share `DON_AGE`, `DON_CREAT`, `DON_RACE` and dozens
more. Joining the full files keeps both copies, renamed with `.x` and `.y`
suffixes, and the two can differ: each file records the value from its own
form. Decide which file you take each column from, and drop or rename the
other copy before joining.

The two files also share `PERS_ID`, but it is not the same attribute: in
the transplant file it identifies the recipient, and in the donor file it
has its own meaning (read its label in the dictionary). Never pick one copy
for the other. Rename the donor file's copy, for example to
`DONOR_PERS_ID`, or drop it, before any join.

For a column that measures the same thing in both files, such as donor
age:

```{r overlap}
tx_with_age <- tx |> mutate(DON_AGE = c(41, 22, 40, 61, NA, 30, 45))

joined <- left_join(tx_with_age, donors, by = "DONOR_ID",
                    relationship = "many-to-one", na_matches = "never")
names(joined)

# Keep the transplant file's donor age; take nothing else from donors here.
joined <- left_join(
  tx_with_age,
  donors |> rename(DON_AGE_DONOR_FILE = DON_AGE),
  by = "DONOR_ID", relationship = "many-to-one", na_matches = "never"
)
sum(joined$DON_AGE != joined$DON_AGE_DONOR_FILE, na.rm = TRUE)
```

On real files, count such disagreements, masked, before you choose.

# Transplants are not people

```{r people}
c(
  transplants = n_distinct(tx$TRR_ID),
  people = n_distinct(tx$PERS_ID)
)
```

Person 1 counts twice as a transplant, and person 3 three times. Decide
which unit your analysis
needs:

- **Every transplant**, as in graft survival. Repeat transplants are
  correlated, so say how the analysis allows for that.
- **First transplant per person**, as in many patient survival analyses.
  Keep the earliest transplant date per person:

```{r first-tx}
first_tx <- tx |>
  filter(!is.na(PERS_ID), !is.na(REC_TX_DT)) |>
  slice_min(REC_TX_DT, by = PERS_ID, with_ties = TRUE)

first_tx |>
  count(PERS_ID) |>
  summarise(
    people = n(),
    people_with_same_day_ties = sum(n > 1)
  ) |>
  mutate(set_aside = sum(is.na(tx$PERS_ID) | is.na(tx$REC_TX_DT)))
```

Rows with a missing person or date are set aside and counted, not grouped
together. `with_ties = TRUE` keeps every registration on a person's
earliest date, so same-day ties stay visible; decide how to handle them
before the cohort is final (a multi-organ transplant is one cause; see
below).

The first transplant in your file may not be the person's first ever: the
file covers a fixed period, and a person may have had a transplant of
another organ. Transplant files record previous transplants in
`CAN_PREV_TX`, and previous kidney transplants in `REC_PREV_KI`.

# Donors and recipients

The join from transplants to donors is many to one: one deceased donor can
give a kidney to one recipient and a liver to another, so the same
`DONOR_ID` appears in `TX_KI` and `TX_LI`. Count donors as distinct
`DONOR_ID`s, never as rows of a transplant file.

Living donors are in `DONOR_LIVE`, not `DONOR_DECEASED`. A transplant
file's `DON_TY` says which: `"C"` for a deceased donor, `"L"` for a living
one. So when you join a transplant file to `DONOR_DECEASED`, transplants
from living donors find no match. Filter on `DON_TY` first, or join each
donor file to its own transplants.

# Organs and multi-organ transplants

Each organ has its own transplant and follow-up files. Kidney-pancreas
transplants have their own pair of files, `TX_KP` and `TXF_KP`, and each
graft has its own follow-up dates.

Files that cover several organs, such as `CAND_KIPA` (kidney and pancreas
listings), need filtering to the organ you study. Transplant files list
the organs involved in each transplant in `REC_TX_ORG_TY`.

A multi-organ transplant can have a registration in each organ's file.
`TX_ID` identifies the transplant event and, by its dictionary label, is
the same across organs. So before you combine organ files, keep the source
file and compare distinct registrations with distinct transplant events:

```{r multi-organ}
tx_ki <- tibble(
  TRR_ID = c(201, 202, 203, 204),
  TX_ID = c(9001, 9002, 9004, 9004),
  PERS_ID = c(5, 6, 7, 7)
)
tx_li <- tibble(TRR_ID = c(301, 302), TX_ID = c(9002, 9003), PERS_ID = c(6, 5))

both <- bind_rows(TX_KI = tx_ki, TX_LI = tx_li, .id = "file")
files_per_event <- both |>
  filter(!is.na(TX_ID)) |>
  distinct(TX_ID, file) |>
  count(TX_ID, name = "files")
c(
  registrations = n_distinct(both$TRR_ID),
  transplant_events = n_distinct(both$TX_ID),
  events_in_more_than_one_file = sum(files_per_event$files > 1)
)
```

Transplant event 9002 is a kidney-liver transplant for person 6, with one
registration in each file. Event 9004 has two registrations in the kidney
file alone, so it does not count as shared across files; whether that can
happen on real files is one of the things to check. Person 5 appears in
both files too, but for two separate transplants: a repeated `PERS_ID`
alone does not mean a multi-organ transplant. Whether `TX_ID` is the same across files, and
whether `TRR_ID` ever repeats across them, should be checked on your own
release before you rely on it.

# Load less

Large files load faster when you select columns, and you can keep only the
follow-up forms of the transplants you study:

```{r load, eval = FALSE}
tx <- sRtr::load_srtr_file("TX_KI", col_select = c("TRR_ID", "PERS_ID",
                                                  "DONOR_ID", "REC_TX_DT"))
txf <- sRtr::load_srtr_file("TXF_KI", trr_id_filter = tx$TRR_ID,
                            col_select = c("TRR_ID", "TRR_FOL_ID",
                                           "TFL_PX_STAT_DT"))
```

`trr_id_filter` limits the rows returned, not what is read; `col_select`
reads less. See [Getting started](getting-started.html#join-files-on-their-keys).

# Checklist

- Name the unit of every count: registration, person, transplant, form,
  donor or center.
- Before a join, check the key is complete and unique on the side that
  should have one row per key.
- Use `by`, `relationship =` and `na_matches = "never"` in dplyr joins, and
  compare row counts before and after.
- Choose which file each shared column comes from.
- Explain unmatched rows rather than dropping them silently.
- Share counts only, masked.
